You may extend it to at most 10 hours, but no more than twice in the same week.
Your driving must also stay within two other limits: no more than 56 hours in the week, and no more than 90 hours in total over any two consecutive weeks.
The weekly driving must also not push you over the maximum weekly working time set by Directive 2002/15/EC.

sentences: Your next weekly rest must start no later than at the end of six 24-hour periods (144 hours) after the end of your previous weekly rest.
Over any two weeks in a row you need either two regular weekly rests, or one regular weekly rest and one reduced weekly rest of at least 24 hours.
Exception: if you do international goods transport, you may take two reduced weekly rests in a row outside your Member State of establishment.
In that case you must take at least four weekly rests in any four consecutive weeks, and at least two of them must be regular.

As an exception, a Member State may issue a temporary card that cannot be renewed and is valid for at most 185 days.

Compensation for night work is set by national law, collective agreements or national practice, but it must not endanger road safety.
You also still need breaks: you may not work more than 6 hours in a row without a break.
The break must be at least 30 minutes if you work between 6 and 9 hours in total, and at least 45 minutes if you work more than 9 hours.

sentences: Possibly, but only in limited cases.

Commission guidance note 4 (March 2015, older than the 2020 Mobility Package) says enforcers may allow a tolerance of up to 15 minutes per 4.5-hour block of driving for vehicles on frequent-stop or multi-drop journeys.
For example, they might deduct one minute per driving block between stops, up to 15 minutes per block.
Conditions:
- It is a transitional tolerance.
It only covers digital tachographs activated before October 2011 that do not comply with Regulation 1266/2009, which made recording more accurate.
- You must be able to back it up with evidence, such as verifiable proof of frequent or multi-drop stops.
- It is at the control officer's discretion and must not undermine the drivers' hours rules or road safety.
- It applies only where the journey clearly involves frequent or multi-stop operations.
Whenever you are behind the wheel on an in-scope operation, you count as driving, even in a traffic jam or at traffic lights.

sentences: Periods of availability are periods that are neither breaks nor rest, when you don't have to stay at your workstation but must be ready to answer calls to start or resume driving or to do other work.
They include time spent accompanying a vehicle carried by ferry or train, waiting at frontiers, and waiting because of traffic bans.

You must know these periods and how long they are likely to last in advance: either before departure or just before the period starts, or under general conditions agreed between the social partners and/or national law.
For team drivers, time spent sitting next to the driver or on the couchette while the vehicle is moving also counts as availability.

sentences: Under Directive 2002/15/EC you are a "self-employed driver" only if you meet all of these conditions:
- your main occupation is carrying passengers or goods by road for hire or reward, under a Community licence or other professional authorisation;
- you are entitled to work for yourself;
- you are not tied to an employer by an employment contract or any other working hierarchical relationship;
- you are free to organise your own work;
- your income depends directly on the profits made;
- you are free to have business with several customers, alone or through a cooperation with other self-employed drivers.
If you do not meet these criteria, you are treated like a mobile worker: same obligations, same rights.
The Directive applies to self-employed drivers from 23 March 2009.

sentences: Yes.
You can take a regular daily rest in two parts: the first must be an uninterrupted period of at least 3 hours and the second an uninterrupted period of at least 9 hours.
Within 24 hours after the end of your previous daily or weekly rest, you must have taken a new daily rest.
If the part of your daily rest that falls within that 24-hour period is at least 9 but less than 11 hours, it counts as a reduced daily rest.
You may have at most three reduced daily rests between any two weekly rests.

Ferry or train with a bunk or couchette: according to the Commission's guidance note from 2017 (older than the current Regulation), a regular daily rest taken on board may be interrupted at most twice.
This limit of two applies to the whole daily rest, not to each of the two parts.

Article 8(2) requires a new daily rest within each 24 hours after the end of the previous daily or weekly rest.
Article 8(2) states that a portion of at least nine but less than 11 hours within the 24-hour period is regarded as a reduced daily rest.
Article 8(4) states that a driver may have at most three reduced daily rests between any two weekly rests.

The guidance note states that the maximum of two interruptions concerns the whole daily rest and not each part of a split rest.

sentences: Yes.
When you drive in a multi-manning crew, you may take your 45-minute break in the vehicle while the other driver is driving.
The condition is that you do not help the driver who is driving during that time.
Multi-manning means that, between two consecutive daily rest periods (or between a daily and a weekly rest), there are at least two drivers in the vehicle to do the driving.
The second driver only has to be on board after the first hour.

sentences: A Member State may exempt these vehicles from the rules on driving times, breaks and rest periods (Articles 5 to 9 of Regulation 561/2006).
It may do so only if the objectives of Article 1 are not prejudiced, and the exemption applies on its own territory, or on another Member State's territory if that State agrees.
The Member State may attach individual conditions.
The exemption covers a vehicle or combination only if all of these apply:
- its maximum permissible mass does not exceed 7,5 tonnes;
- it is used by a universal service provider (as defined in the Postal Directive 97/67/EC) to deliver items as part of the universal service;
- it is used only within a 100 km radius of the undertaking's base;
- driving is not the driver's main activity.
Member States may also exempt these vehicles from the tachograph rules of Regulation 165/2014.

Note that Clarification note 3 (2007) predates the 2020 changes and describes a different, older wording of Article 13(1)(d) (50 km radius, carrying material or equipment), so follow the current Regulation.

Also, one card or record sheet may not be used to cover a period longer than the one it is intended for.

sentences: Not just by renewing the urgent exception on its own.
A Member State can grant an urgent temporary exception for at most 30 days, and it must notify the Commission straight away.
If the crisis continues beyond 30 days, the Member State can ask the Commission for authorisation under Article 14(1) to extend the relaxation of certain rules.
That longer exception can only cover Articles 6 to 9 (driving times, breaks and rest periods), and only if the Regulation's objectives are not harmed.
The clarification note dates from 2012, before the 2020 Mobility Package, but this point matches the current text of the Regulation.

sentences: No, you cannot be required to carry one.
According to Commission clarification note 7, Article 34(3) of Regulation (EU) No 165/2014 forbids Member States from imposing the form that attests a driver's activities while away from the vehicle.
Enforcement authorities should not penalise drivers for not having such a form.
Instead, you should record your time away from the vehicle, including annual leave, as manual entries on the tachograph on the day you next use it.
Your records must cover every day of the checked period.
If manual entry is technically impossible, for example with a 1st generation digital tachograph, or is excessively burdensome, you may choose to use the standard attestation form.
Authorities are recommended to accept it in such cases.
Guidance note 5 (2013) is older and said only that Member States were not obliged to require the form, while still forbidding any form for ordinary daily or weekly rest.
Both notes were published before the 2020 Mobility Package changed the rules, and the text of Article 34 itself is not among these passages.

sentences: Yes.
According to Commission clarification note 5, a bus driver who mixes regular services must keep tachograph records whichever type of driving is predominant.
Regular passenger services on routes of 50 km or less fall outside Regulation 561/2006.
When you drive those short routes, record the time as "other work" on the tachograph, not as driving time.
On journeys over 50 km, record "driving time" as normal.
The out-of-scope driving does not count as rest and must be taken into account when the rules are applied to you.
Note that this guidance dates from July 2007, before the 2020 Mobility Package changed the rules, and the passages do not show whether the current acts say anything different on this point.

sentences: If you drive a vehicle that falls outside Regulation 561/2006 to or from a vehicle that falls within it, and that in-scope vehicle is not at your home or at the employer's operational centre where you are normally based, the time counts as other work, not as rest or a break.
You must record it as other work.
More generally, any time spent driving a vehicle used for commercial operations outside the Regulation's scope is recorded as other work.
You enter this record either manually on a record sheet or printout, or by using the manual input facilities on the recording equipment (tachograph).

sentences: Yes.
Under Regulation 561/2006, a daily rest period may be extended so that it becomes a regular weekly rest period or a reduced weekly rest period.
Keep in mind that a regular weekly rest (and any weekly rest over 45 hours taken as compensation for earlier reduced weekly rests) must not be taken in the vehicle.
It must be taken in suitable gender-friendly accommodation with adequate sleeping and sanitary facilities, paid for by the employer.

sentences: When two or more drivers crew the vehicle, you can take your 45-minute break while sitting in the vehicle as your colleague drives.
The condition is that you are not helping the driver drive (for example, not navigating or assisting).
The Commission's 2007 guidance note, which predates the 2020 Mobility Package, describes the time you sit next to the driver, ready to drive when needed, as your 'period of availability'.
Of that time, 45 minutes can be treated as a break.
The current Regulation also allows the 45-minute break in a vehicle driven by another driver.

sentences: Working: under the working time rules for mobile workers you must never work more than 6 hours in a row without a break.
If your working hours total between 6 and 9 hours, you need a break of at least 30 minutes.
If they total more than 9 hours, you need at least 45 minutes.
Driving: after 4½ hours of driving you must take an uninterrupted break of at least 45 minutes, unless you take a rest period instead.
You can split this break into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30 minutes, spread over the driving period.
Exceptions:
- On an occasional passenger service, you can instead take two breaks of at least 15 minutes each.
- In multi-manning, you can take your 45-minute break in the moving vehicle, as long as you are not helping the person driving.

Guidance note 6 says the derogation does not apply to any weekly rest period.
That note dates from January 2017, before the 2020 Mobility Package, and is outdated: follow the current Regulation.

sentences: No.
A rest of at least 45 hours counts as a regular weekly rest, and a regular weekly rest may not be taken in the vehicle.
The same applies to any weekly rest of more than 45 hours taken as compensation for earlier reduced weekly rests.
You must take it in suitable, gender-friendly accommodation with proper sleeping and sanitary facilities, and your employer must pay for that accommodation.
There is one exception: if you travel with your vehicle on a ferry or train, a regular weekly rest may be taken during that crossing.
The journey must be scheduled for 8 hours or more, and you must have access to a sleeper cabin on the ferry or train.
That means a sleeper cabin on board, not your truck cab.

sentences: Yes.
Since 2 February 2022, when you cross a border of a Member State, you must enter the symbol of the country you are entering at the start of your first stop in that Member State.
That first stop must be at the nearest possible stopping place at or after the border.
If you cross on a ferry or train, enter the country symbol at the port or station of arrival.
You must also enter the country symbols where your daily working period started and where it finished.
